Göran Ravnsborg, a university lecturer in law, is a Swedish citizen and lives in Lund in Sweden. He held a power of attorney from his adoptive mother, Mrs Karin Schieck, and, on 19 November 1982, he was appointed administrator (god man) for her friend, Mrs Marie Åkerblom. As both Mrs Schiecks became unable to care for themselves because of their advanced age, they were placed in a nursing home by the Municipality of Göteborg. The nursing home charged them for medical care and the applicant effected the relevant payments. When he subsequently realised that the nursing home was a charitable association, he stopped paying the fees on the ground that the institution in question was not entitled to charge them.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32848/06) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. By a decision of 9 October 2007 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant submitted his claims for just satisfaction. The Government made their comments on that matter. The decision was made by the Court of Appeal and was delivered by the judge, Mr Torben Moesgaard Petersen (“the applicant”), on 1 August 2006. Copenhagen City Court granted police a warrant to search the premises of the applicant’s business and those of the company. The applicant was charged on forty-four counts out of a total of fifty-nine, committed between 26 June and 3 November 1992. His responsibility related to an amount of DKK 87,000,000 equal to approximately 11,600,000 euros (EUR) out of the total tax amount evaded in the case. The indictment related to eighty different companies and six banks in Denmark and abroad. More than seventy witnesses were heard, including state-registered public accountants. The court records comprised 1,330 pages and closing speeches were held over ten days in November. The City Court convicted the applicant in accordance with the indictment. The co-accused were also convicted. The applicant was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. In addition, the sum of DKK 3,600,000 was seized, and he was deprived for an indefinite period of the right to establish a private limited company or a company or an association requiring public approval. The City Court dismissed the applicant’s claim that the length of the proceedings had been at variance with Article 6 of the Convention stating the following: “The. City Court finds no reason to criticise the prosecution's decision to join the criminal. proceedings against the [applicant and the five co‑accused].” The trial commenced on 24 September 2002. Most of the hearings took place in 2003 and 2004. A total of about 90 hearings were held in the case. In February and March 2004 the appeal hearings had to be postponed because a co-defendant fell ill. The closing speeches were held over ten days in April, May, and June 2004. On 28 September 2004 the High Court upheld the City Court’s judgment. In January 2005 the cases were sent to the prosecution, which gave its opinion on 29 March 2005. The applicant and the co‑defendants gave their comments in reply and at a meeting on 5 August 2005 the Leave to Appeal Board decided to refuse the requests. The case came to the attention of the Leave to Appeal Board on 2 May 2006. The police phoned the board and drew attention to the case. The applicant and the co-defendant were informed that their requests for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court had been refused on 21 June 2006. At the same time, the board apologised for the length of the proceedings before it. The case was settled out of court and the applicant was awarded the right to a retrial at a later date. The appeal was dismissed and the case was dismissed out of Court of Appeal. The application was overturned on appeal on 14 July 2006.

The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section of the Court.  Hueth Wilson was sentenced to life imprisonment for buggery of a young girl in 1977. His tariff period (the minimum period of detention satisfying the requirements of retribution and deterrence) was set at six years and expired in April 1989. His time in prison was characterised by periods of thought disorder, delusions and behavioural problems and the Secretary of State decided that he was in need of care and treatment in a secure hospital. In August 1989, he was made the subject of a transfer direction and a restriction order under, respectively, sections 47 and 49 of the Mental Health Act 1983 (the 1983 Act) and transferred to Broadmoor Special Hospital. In April 1994, the first applicant was transferred to Bracton Clinic Regional Secure Unit. On 9 January 2001, the MHR Tribunal recommended his discharge. The applicants were not eligible for review by the discretionary lifer panels empowered by section 34 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 to order their release on licence. The rights to a hearing under the 1991 Act were conferred only on persons who were solely subject to that Act, and not on those who were mental patients. In June 1993, following consultation with the trial judge and the Lord Chief Justice, the Secretary of State decided that the second applicant should be regarded as a “technical lifer”. On appeal, on 19 July 1994, the Court of Appeal reversed the High Court's decision in part. The applicants were informed by letter of 18 May 1995 that the House of Lords had refused leave to appeal.

Two detective police officers left Limerick city in an unmarked police car escorting a post office van carrying significant sums of money on its way to Adare village, Co. Limerick. When the two vehicles arrived at the post office in Adare, the police car was rammed from behind by a stolen vehicle and immediately surrounded by five heavily armed and masked individuals dressed in paramilitary style uniforms. One of the five opened fire at point blank range on the police officers and one of those officers died instantly. The police suspected a local unit of the Irish Republican Army (an unlawful paramilitary organisation known as the IRA) and the IRA later claimed responsibility for the murder.

The application was heard before the Divisional Court on 21 and 22 March 2001, together with the application for judicial review of two other prisoners, Mr Pearson and Mr Feal-Martinez. The cases before the European Commission of Human Rights and this Court were also reviewed. Lord Justice Kennedy concluded: “... I return to the applicant’s case.

The Working Group said that such prisoners had lost the moral authority to vote. Parliament in this country could have provided differently in order to meet the objectives which it discerned. It is easy to be critical of a law which operates against a wide spectrum (e.g. in relation to its effect on post-tariff discretionary life prisoners, and those detained under some provision of the Mental Health Act 1983) But its position in the spectrum is plainly a matter for Parliament not for the courts. That applies even to the ‘hard cases’, such as those under Mental health Act 1983, which can be difficult to implement.

Convicted prisoners have forfeited their right to have a say in the way the country is governed. The Working Group said that such prisoners had lost the moral authority to vote. Parliament in this country could have provided differently in order to meet the objectives which it discerned, and like McLachlin J in Canada, I would accept that the tailoring process seldom admits of perfection, so the courts must afford some leeway to the legislator. That applies even to the ‘hard’ cases, such as that in Mathieu-Mohin. The European Court also requires that the means employed to restrict the implied Convention rights to vote are not disproportionate, and that is the point at which it is appropriate for this court to defer to the legislature.

From 20 August 1991 the applicant was treated by the chief psychiatrist who drew her attention to the possible detrimental effect her situation might have on her son. The psychiatrist advised her to seek support for him from the children's psychiatric clinic or the social authorities.

The applicant's son was placed in a non-residential therapeutic school on 2 March 1992. The headmaster and a teacher had expressed concern about his learning difficulties and his general state of health. In October 1991 they had contacted the Social Council and expressed concern. Following this, the Council commenced an investigation which, with Mrs Andersson's agreement, led to the placement of her son in the therapeutic school. The application was dismissed by the judge on the grounds that the boy was not mentally ill and that he did not consider himself mentally ill. The judge ruled that the application should be dismissed on the basis that the child had been placed in the non-residents' therapeutic school because he was in the care of a psychiatric clinic and not a social welfare agency.

The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (Art. 6-3-c). The applicant indicated in a letter postmarked 22 July 1993 that he did not wish to take part in the proceedings. On 17 November 1993 he submitted a claim for just satisfaction.

Peter Maxwell was found guilty of assault and sentenced to five years in prison. He appealed the conviction on the grounds that he had not been able to substantiate his contention that a crucial witness was giving false evidence against him. The appeal also claimed that there had been insufficient evidence to establish that the assault had resulted in the victim’s permanent disfigurement. Mr Maxwell's legal advisers had disregarded instructions which he had given them and had not defended him in accordance with his instructions. The hearing of his appeal was adjourned and Mr Maxwell was given a chance to appeal his conviction. He lodged with the court a note of appeal setting out grounds which he formulated himself. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of Mr Maxwell.

Peter Maxwell was convicted of assault in the High Court of Justiciary at Kilmarnock, Scotland. The judge sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. Mr Maxwell instructed a new firm of solicitors, who then asked counsel who had represented him at the trial to advise on the prospects of an appeal. Having received counsel’s advice, the solicitors informed the applicant that they could not identify any basis for an appeal and accordingly could not act for him. The applicant lodged with the court a note of appeal setting out grounds which he formulated himself. The grounds of appeal can be summarised as follows: (a) the applicant had not been able to substantiate his contention that a crucial witness was giving false evidence against him because to do so would have involved revealing to the jury a previous conviction; (b) a number of witnesses had not be called by the Crown or by the Defence; (c) crucial evidence had been entirely fabricated.

Peter Maxwell was sentenced to five years' imprisonment for assault. He was found guilty by a jury in May 1990 and given a five-year sentence. He appealed the sentence on the grounds that the evidence against him had been fabricated and that his legal advisers had not defended him in accordance with his instructions. The appeal hearing was adjourned and Mr Maxwell instructed a new firm of solicitors. Shortly before the adjourned hearing, those solicitors informed the applicant that they could no longer act for him. Mr Maxwell lodged with the court a note of appeal setting out grounds which he had formulated himself. The applicant was found not guilty by the jury on 29 May 1990.

Mr Maxwell’s solicitors submitted to the Board that their client should nonetheless be granted legal aid in view of the lengthy sentence which he had received. His solicitors advised him that he should abandon his appeal but he chose not to accept their advice. On 21 March 1991, the applicant addressed the High Court of Justiciary on his grounds of appeal. Presiding over the three-judge bench was the Lord Justice Clerk, one of the two most senior judges in Scotland. On the same date the court dismissed the appeal. The applicant decided to proceed with his appeal personally. The appeal was dismissed and the Crown was represented by counsel but there is no indication that he intervened at the hearing.

On 25 January 1991, the Board informed Mr Maxwell that his application had been refused as the Board was not satisfied, as it was required to be under the relevant legislation, that there were substantial grounds for making an appeal. His solicitors advised him that he should abandon his appeal but he chose not to accept their advice. The applicant decided to proceed with his appeal personally.

Peter Maxwell, a British citizen born in 1944, was found guilty of assault. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 April 1994. Legal aid had been made available to the applicant for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides and Lord Rodger as well as replies to its questions. The grounds of appeal can be summarised as follows: (a) the applicant had not been able to substantiate his contention that a crucial witness was giving false evidence against him because to do so would have involved revealing to the jury a previous conviction; (b) a number of witnesses had not be called by the Crown or by the Defence; (c) crucial evidence had been entirely fabricated; (d) the verdict of the jury was not supported by the evidence; (e) his legal advisers had disregarded instructions which he had given them and had not defended him in accordance with his instructions. name: Ayhan Çakmak
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 53672/00) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52): the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26: the Court declared the application admissible on 23 September 2003. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25: 1) The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59: 1).

The case originated in an application (no. 53672/00) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Two Turkish nationals, Mr Ayhan Çakmak and Mrs Süreyya Çkmak (‘the applicants’) complained about the length of compensation proceedings. The applicants were represented by Mr O.K. Cengiz, a lawyer practising in Izmir. By a decision of 23 September 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section.

The case originated in an application (no. 53672/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Turkish nationals. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court. By a decision of 23 September 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1), and the case was dismissed.

The applicants' daughter, C.Ç., was severely injured in an accident in 1987. Her hair was burned and part of her scalp was damaged. In 1992 she underwent surgery to repair the damage to her scalp. Following the operation, her physical appearance did not improve. The applicants filed an action with the Izmir Civil Court of First Instance against the doctors who performed the operation. They claimed compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary loss sustained as a result of medical malpractice. The court dismissed the applicants' claim for compensation on the ground that it was not competent to examine the acts of civil servants.

The applicants' daughter, C.Ç., was severely injured in an accident in 1987. She underwent surgery at the Ege University Plastic Surgery Department to repair the damage to her scalp. Following the operation, she caught an infection. The applicants filed an action with the Izmir Civil Court of First Instance against the doctors who performed the operation. They claimed compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary loss sustained as a result of medical malpractice. The court dismissed the applicants' claim for compensation on the ground that it was not competent to examine the acts of civil servants carried out in the exercise of their duties. The Izmir Administrative Court, relying on the experts' conclusions, found that there was no indication of any negligence.

The applicants' daughter, C.Ç., was severely injured in an accident in 1987. Her hair was burned and part of her scalp was damaged. She underwent surgery at the Ege University Plastic Surgery Department to repair the damage to her scalp. Prior to the operation, the doctors informed the applicants about the risks involved. The applicants filed an action with the Izmir Civil Court of First Instance against the doctors who performed the operation. They claimed compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary loss sustained as a result of medical malpractice. The Izmir Administrative Court, relying on the experts' conclusions, found that there was no indication of any negligence on the part of the Medical Department.

The applicants appealed against the judgment of the first-instance court. The Supreme Administrative Court, without holding a hearing, dismissed the applicants' appeal. name: Hıdır Adıyaman
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31880/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. Mr Rıza Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28) The Government appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court decided the case should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State.

The case originated in an application (no. 31880/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court decided that the application was not valid.

The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) On 19 October 1981 the Ankara Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. On 18 May 1987 the applicant was released pending trial. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the martial law court convicted the applicant. It sentenced the applicant to 12 years’ imprisonment under Article 146 § 3 of the Turkish Criminal Code, permanently debarred him from employment in the civil service. On 27 December 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed the applicant's conviction. It referred the case to the Ankara Assize Court. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the latter court.

The case involves the arrest and detention of the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court convicted the applicant of membership. It sentenced the applicant to 12 years’ imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in the civil service. In 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi). It referred the case to the latter court.

On 31 August 1981 police officers from the Ankara Security Directorate arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) On 19 October 1981 the Ankara Martial Law Court (sıkıyönetim mahkemesi) ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. On 18 May 1987 the applicant was released pending trial. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court convicted the applicant of membership. The applicant was sentenced to 12 years’ imprisonment under Article 146 § 3 of the Turkish Criminal Code, permanently debarred him from employment in the civil service. The case is still pending before the Ankara Assize Court.

The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties the parties were granted leave to appeal. The case was brought against the applicant by the Ankara Security Directorate. He was accused of membership of the Dev-Yol, a Marxist-Leninist organisation. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction on the ground that he should have been convicted of the offence. The criminal proceedings are still pending before the Ankara Assize Court (ağır ceza mahkemesi). The case file was transmitted to the latter court on 26 December 1994. The applicant appealed the conviction and it was quashed on 27 December 1995. The case is still pending.

name: Murat Kılıç
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40498/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal due to the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Ankara State Security Court. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 8 July 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. It retained the applicant’s complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the court which tried and convicted him.

The case originated in an application (no. 40498/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal due to the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Ankara State Security Court. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. By a decision of 8 July 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. It retained the applicant’s complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the court which tried and convicted him and declared inadmissible the remainder of his complaints.

The case originated in an application (no. 40498/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Ankara. On 18 October 1992 the applicant was arrested by police officers from the Ankara Security Directorate following a search conducted in his house. On 2 November 1992 the public prosecutor laid charges against the applicant and six other persons for having formed an illegal organisation (“Partiye Rizgariye Kurdistan”: hereinafter “PRK”) The applicant and his co-accused were also charged with distributing illegal leaflets and carrying identification cards and driving licences belonging to third parties. The court sentenced the applicant to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment and debarred them from public service indefinitely. On 7 October 1997 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Ankara. On 18 October 1992 the applicant was arrested by police officers from the Ankara Security Directorate following a search conducted in his house. On 2 November 1992 the public prosecutor laid charges against the applicant and six other persons for having formed an illegal organisation. The applicant and four of his co-accused were sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment and debarred them from public service indefinitely. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 7 October 1997. The case was heard at the Ankara State Security Court and the trial was adjourned until 14 November 1997.

The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Ankara. He was arrested by police officers from the Ankara Security Directorate following a search conducted in his house. The court found the applicant and four of his co-accused guilty of an offence under Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act. They were sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment and debarred from public service indefinitely. The applicant appealed. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 7 October 1997. The case against the applicant was decided by the Ankara State Security Court on 7 November 1996.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40498/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal due to the presence of a military judge on the bench. The Court declared the application partly admissible. It retained the applicant’s complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the Ankara State Security Court which tried and convicted him. The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court. The Government and the applicant each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Ankara State Security Court found the applicant and four of his co-accused guilty of an offence under Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act. The search of their houses had uncovered the internal regulations of the party whose aim was to establish an independent Kurdish State on the territory of the Turkish State through dissemination of propaganda. The court also noted that the aim of theparty was to set up by means of force an independent socialist and united State of Kurdistan within the territories of Iran, Iraq and Syria. The applicant was sentenced to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment and debarred from public service indefinitely.

The applicant was found guilty of twelve counts of corruption in 1993. A confiscation Order was made against him in the amount of GPB 1,503,301.80. He was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment under section 1 of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1906 on each of the twelve counts, to be served concurrently. The applicant did not dispute before the Court of Appeal that he had realisable assets in excess of GBP 1.27 million. The High Court appointed the Receiver under section 80(2) of the 1988 Act on application by the applicant. Ms S.D. was appointed as Receiver to realise the applicant’s property.

Ms S.D. was appointed as Receiver to realise the applicant’s property, including any property of the applicant held by third parties. The applicant did not dispute before the Court of Appeal that he had realisable assets in excess of GBP 1.27 million. The applicant was declared bankrupt on 2 September 1996. Ms S.D. was appointed as the applicant’s Trustee in Bankruptcy. This appointment was independent of her appointment as Receiver. The Order was made under section 371 of the Insolvency Act 1986. Between 27 September 1996 and 10 January 1997, a total of 71 letters addressed to the applicant were re-directed to the Receiver and Trustee. These letters included, inter alia, a letter from the Chief Inspector of the Ministry of Defence Police, two letters from the Legal Aid Board concerning civil proceedings to which the applicant was a party. The application was based on the grounds that the Trustee was of the opinion that communications concerning remittances and useful information in respect of the applicant's assets and liabilities might be forwarded.

The applicant complained that apparently privileged material was being intercepted.
